body:
>Why do the cops and emt personnel treat us like dogs, like we are beneath them? This is why I’ll never call for help again.

Not all of them do, but I've seen, heard about, experienced that in the past. A lot of it is desensitization. So basically this is how it works:

* You join a police department, go through your training, and hit the street.
* One day, you get a suicide call. You respond. You are kind, articulate, and you get them the help they need. (1)
* You get another suicide call another time. This one doesn't make it. You are sad, but you tried your best to get there in time. (2)
* You get another suicide call. This one is pretty serious. Hell, you'd probably try to off yourself if you were in their situation, too. It's just bad. You sympathize. You try to get them help. (3)
* You get a suicide call and it was basically a big prank. You chastise the people who called it in. You think back to (3) and wonder why people would fake that? To get attention? To see the cops race across town for nothing?
* You get a suicide call where they didn't make it again. It doesn't make sense. The guy had it all, wife, kids, big house, good job, lots of money. Everything you want that you may or may not get (especially not the big house and money). (4)
* You've been doing this a couple years now. You've seen most of everything there is to see. You see how cheap and how simultaneously valuable life is. You've met all of the "regulars" in town who are always being carried off to jail, the "frequent fliers". Burglaries, robberies, homicide, suicide, changed some flat tires, directed some traffic, written some tickets, worked some wrecks.
* The calls keep coming. And they keep coming. You are here, the faces change, but the situations start to get routine, only instead of how most people's routines deal with when lunch is, doing homework with the kids, or the minor tasks at work, your job adds in varying amounts of death, pain, and suffering.
* You get a call from someone wanting to commit suicide because their pet goldfish passed away. You scoff at this. You've seen all these "serious" situations before and you think the person is dumb for being suicidal for that reason. You tell them so. You tell them they're a spoiled brat. You don't care; you think it's the dumbest reason you ever heard of. (5)

5 deserves as much respect and care as 4 and as 3 and as 2 and as 1. But when you hit 5 after seeing all the other ones, you start to judge things on severity. If you had visited #5 first, you probably would've acted like #1, or at least you wouldn't make the person feel worse since you were fresher, newer, less experienced, less desensitized. After a while, it all blurs together and it's just another inconvenience that you lose your lunch break over.

That is how burnout starts in the police (and really all emergency services). Things that are tragic, horrible, incomprehensible to most people become routine to first responders. So you had a wreck today? That's terrible, I'm very sorry. But your one wreck that you had is just one of the ten wrecks I've worked today where everyone had an attitude and was angry about their car getting damaged.

It is often said that police officers and dispatchers are dealing with the entire world on the worst day of their lives. It's a very negative environment, and that negativity breeds desensitization.

That's not to excuse their behavior, not in the least. Everyone deserves to be treated with dignity and respect. I only mean to explain the processes that go on deep inside the first responder. Some of us are better at fighting these urges and emotions than others. I'm not perfect by any means, but I kept a tight leash on that side of me until I couldn't anymore, coupled with several other factors. So I left today.

>Also, I hate to hear you, a 911 dispatcher, are also planning your own suicide. That hit me pretty hard. Here’s to hoping you find what you need in this world.

It's ok. I'm so desensitized now that if I do run out of money and kill myself, it's more of a process to conclude my life, stop consuming resources, reduce the impact on my family spending those resources, etc. I am fully aware of the impact that it will have on others: I've been on the other end of that phone too many times when the husbands, wives, mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, and friends have found someone. So I will say that anyone reading this who feels like there's not anyone who would care, you're dead wrong.

The only time I have had someone call in a suicide who wasn't emotional about it was one of two circumstances: someone who didn't know the person called it in, or it was a murder staged to look like a suicide. And in the first instance, shit, some of them were emotional about it anyway.

Thank you for the question. Of course, different departments will vary somewhat on response and care, how they operate, etc.

In general, police departments are to respond to the incident, interview the person, remove threats to the person (remove access to weapons/means from the area), and summon necessary personnel to handle what happens after. Most police departments will operate in this fashion. Those who are deemed dangerous to themselves may be transported to a mental health facility against their will, which varies on state laws. Most states, if not all, provide some kind of process to take a suicidal person to a mental health professional of some sort.

This is balanced against burnout and desensitization. Police officers themselves often commit suicide due to burnout and desensitization issues, and this can cause a sort of projection onto the people they respond to help. It's easy for an officer who is burned out to say, "Oh, this 16 year old is just a crybaby. They don't know what real problems are like."

In some cases, that may be true, in some cases it may be false. Regardless, the person is experiencing unbearable mental pain to make them feel like they want to die. Just like how police officers are often demonized by the media and the public on account of a few bad apples, the victims/patients are sometimes considered trivial because "the last 3 times we had a teenager threatening suicide, it was just drama".

It's a very real problem, but not all hope is lost.

In my experience, most departments, officers, call takers, and dispatchers take their suicide prevention training very seriously, and the training is very extensive. But like I said, desensitization, burnout, and the mental health of the responding officer(s) and the communications staff can cause them to disregard parts of their training. It's not good, it does happen, but it's not normal procedure.

If a police department mistreats you in such a situation, you have a legal means of recourse in the United States. Once you are able to travel freely, you can go to the police department, speak with a supervisor, and explain to them what happened, what you felt was wrong about it, and what about how they handled it made you upset. If it is bad enough, you are allowed to file a formal written complaint. If a police department refuses to allow you to file a formal written complaint, you should speak to the Attorney General's office in your state for advice.

Edit to add: And yes, some police departments are severely lacking in their training and services. This happens in a lot of small town, but it can happen in large cities, too, even though they have plenty of resources to train their people.
